cases.rationale: The broad claim and consequence are useful, but the wording reads like a compressed planning summary and does not make the body-energy link plainly enough.
Several causal claims are stacked into a list and semicolon, making the spoken explanation feel compressed rather than easy to follow.
A concrete everyday scene with natural rhythm; it gives the child something specific to picture before the lesson explains the consequence.
Direct explanation with familiar verbs and a clear reason that corrects the idea that sitting means the body stops working.
The length earns its place: present-day contrast, Victorian dates, family economics and visible photograph details form one teachable route.
Concrete historical vocabulary is introduced through a person and an action, with specific detail that makes the working condition visible.
As a note fragment it is an abrupt classroom-management cue rather than a comfortable, purposeful spoken line.
The pronoun has no clear noun to refer back to, so the teacher has to repair the sentence while speaking.
It sounds like a teacher speaking, protects pupils from personal disclosure and gives a clear route into the made-up situations.
It sets up the concrete class situation, asks one decision and tells the teacher when pupils should explain their reason.
The child is left to infer what ‘each one’ means and which words count as evidence; the success step needs the action and its object.
Short but runnable: it names the actual feature the child must find in the historical account.
It names the concrete aspect of the evidence to find and preserves the subject distinction between difficulty and danger.
‘No law kept children in school’ is compressed and makes the law sound like an active keeper; the historical point needs a clearer child-facing sentence.
A clear, memorable fact with a concrete age and duration; every part earns its place in the historical takeaway.
The contrast between an immediate effect and a longer-term effect is explicit and easy to retrieve.
Directly asks for the reason the task is designed to evidence, using words a child can act on.
‘Visible detail’ and ‘suggest’ are planning language; the child needs the thing to look at and the claim to make in plain words.
A concrete, human question tied to the times already given; it invites thought without hiding the subject in abstract nouns.
It describes how the resource is assembled rather than showing the child how the evidence supports each part of the answer.
It answers all three parts in attainable language and attaches precise historical quotations to the claims.
A concise model answer that states the decision and names the taught body work that justifies it.
Direct, natural explanation that names the visible cause and uses a normal contraction.
Formal, passive and abstract wording turns a simple explanation into document language.
Short question that names the mathematical decision plainly.
Teacher-talk padding belongs in spoken notes; the printed question can ask the decision directly.
The light narrative opening earns its place and leads into a concrete geographical idea.
Plain definition with the subject term the lesson needs.
The repeated sentence opening creates a mechanical rhythm; the linked climate explanation can be made more natural.
A brief, content-led light line with a clear turn that a teacher could say naturally.
A complete condition that tells the child the next action in the method.
Compressed slogan-like fragments make the child unpack both the condition and the action.
